There's a famous quote about bees.
If the bee disappeared from the face of the Earth, humans would have only four years left to live.
There's just one problem. Einstein never said it.
The earliest version anyone has found appeared in a French magazine in 1965. Ten years after he died.
But the question behind the fake quote is a real one. What would actually happen if every bee disappeared?
The true answer is less like the end of the world, and more like a very strange trip to the supermarket.
Chapter one. What a bee actually does.
Here's the strange part: bees have no idea they're feeding you.
A bee doesn't visit flowers to help us. She's shopping. Nectar for energy, and pollen to feed her young.
But pollen is sticky, and bees are fuzzy. So on every visit, a little golden dust from one flower rides along to the next.
That's pollination. When pollen reaches a flower of the same kind, the flower can swell into a fruit, with seeds inside.
No delivery, and many plants give smaller fruit, misshapen fruit, or no fruit at all.
And bees are not one animal. There are about twenty thousand species of wild bees, from big fuzzy bumblebees to bees smaller than a grain of rice.
The honeybee on your jar of honey is just one of them.
If every bee vanished tonight, what would be missing from your shopping basket tomorrow? Less than you'd think, and more than you'd like.
Imagine walking into a supermarket on the morning after the last bee is gone.
Scientists who studied the world's leading food crops found that eighty-seven of them depend on animal pollination, at least partly. Only twenty-eight don't.
Counted by type, more than three quarters of the world's food crops rely on pollinators, at least partly. Together, they're worth up to five hundred and seventy-seven billion dollars a year.
So start in the fruit aisle. Apples, pears, cherries, melons, blueberries. Fewer of them, and much more expensive.
Then vegetables. Pumpkins, cucumbers, and even the seeds farmers need to grow carrots and onions.
Nuts take a heavy hit, almonds most of all. And your coffee gets a little harder to grow.
But now, look at the other side of the store.
Bread, rice, pasta, cornflakes. Wheat, rice and maize are pollinated by the wind. They don't need a single bee.
That's why, by sheer weight, about sixty percent of the world's food comes from crops that don't need animals at all. Thirty-five percent comes from crops that do.
So we wouldn't run out of calories. We'd run out of colour. The foods that fade away are the ones packed with vitamins.
Could people do a bee's job by hand? In one valley in China, they had to.
To see what that looks like, travel to the mountains of Sichuan, in China.
In Maoxian County, apple and pear trees bloom every spring. But for years, not enough insects came.
Farmers had sprayed pesticides eight to ten times a season, for about four decades. And the forests and grasslands around the valley were turning into farmland.
So, from the late nineteen-eighties, people started doing the bees' job themselves.
They collected flowers, built up a stock of pollen, and climbed into the trees to dab it onto the blossoms, one by one.
A survey in 2001 found that every single apple in Maoxian was pollinated by hand.
And the clock is brutal. The flowers have to be pollinated within about five days of opening.
One person can do five to ten trees a day.
As young workers left for the cities, the cost of that labour rose about tenfold, to twelve to nineteen dollars per person, per day.
Many farmers gave up on apples, and switched to plums, loquats and walnuts.
It made sense. Apples were selling for less than twenty cents a kilo. Plums fetched around two dollars.
Humans can do a bee's job. Just slowly, expensively, and not for long.
Chapter four. One valley, almost every hive.
What if almost every beehive in a country had to visit the same valley? In America, it happens every year.
Now look at the opposite approach. California.
Most of the world's almonds grow in one long valley there. And almond orchards need bees. About two hives for every acre.
So every winter, beekeepers load their hives onto trucks, and drive them in from all over the United States.
For the 2024 bloom, growers needed around two point seven million colonies. That's roughly as many as the entire country counted on the first of January.
The average rent was about a hundred and eighty dollars per hive, for a few weeks of work.
Almond pollination alone earned beekeepers more than three hundred and twenty million dollars in 2024. About eighty percent of all the pollination money in the country.
One crop. One valley. Almost every hive in America.
Could losing pollinators actually make people sick? Researchers tried to put a number on it.
So what would losing all of them really cost us? Not in money. In health.
In 2015, a team of researchers modelled exactly that: a world where every animal pollinator is gone. Not just bees. All of them.
Global fruit supplies fell by about twenty-three percent. Vegetables, by sixteen. Nuts and seeds, by twenty-two.
Seventy-one million more people could become short of vitamin A. A hundred and seventy-three million more, short of folate.
And that's on top of the two point two billion people who already don't get enough vitamin A.
And with fewer fruits and vegetables on the plate, heart disease, strokes, diabetes and some cancers would rise.
Their estimate: about one point four million extra deaths every year. Almost three percent more deaths, worldwide.
It's a model, built on big assumptions. But the direction is clear.
Here's the uncomfortable part. A follow-up study in 2022 estimated that poor pollination is already costing three to five percent of the world's fruit, vegetables and nuts.
That loss is linked to about four hundred and twenty-seven thousand excess deaths a year. Not someday. Now.
Chapter six. Who else is out there?
Do we really need bees at all? Some of your favourite foods don't.
But wait. Our question was about bees. And bees are not the only pollinators.
Take chocolate. The cacao tree's tiny flowers are pollinated by midges. Flies just one to three millimetres long.
So in a world without bees, chocolate would survive. Probably.
Flies, beetles, moths and butterflies visit flowers too. Hummingbirds sip nectar. And at night, bats pollinate agave, the plant behind tequila.
But none of them do the job quite like bees. Bees feed their young on pollen. Their whole bodies are built to collect it.
Losing them wouldn't end life on Earth. It would make it smaller, plainer, and harder.
So, should we panic? Not yet. But the real story is about the bees you've never heard of.
Here's a number that is easy to miss. In the last fifty years, the amount of food we grow from pollinator-dependent crops has gone up by three hundred percent. We need them more than ever.
So, are bees disappearing? Not all at once. Honeybees are kept like livestock, and beekeepers replace the colonies they lose.
The real worry is the wild ones. Where scientists have assessed them, more than forty percent of invertebrate pollinator species, mostly bees and butterflies, face extinction.
The causes are the ones Maoxian learned the hard way. Lost habitat, heavy pesticide use, and a changing climate.
And the fixes are surprisingly simple. Strips of wildflowers along the fields. Fewer, smarter sprays. A corner of the garden left a little wild.
Einstein never warned us about bees. But the quote sticks around for a reason.
So many of the apples, almonds and bright colours on your plate began with a tiny delivery.
